title: Carl Rogers: Self-Actualization Theory
overview: Carl Rogers, a founder of humanistic psychology, built his theory from his work with clients rather than from laboratory research. He saw people as conscious, rational beings driven by one innate motive, the actualization tendency, and understood personality through each person's subjective experiential world. The chapter traces how the self develops in childhood through positive regard, how conditional love creates conditions of worth and incongruence, and what the fully functioning person looks like. It then covers Rogers's optimistic view of human nature, person-centred therapy and encounter groups as assessment methods, Q-sort and other research supporting his ideas, and the criticisms and lasting influence of his work.
objectives: Explain how Rogers's childhood, China trip, breakdown and student clients shaped his theory.
Describe the delinquency research (Kell, McNeil) that made the self central to Rogers's theory.
Explain the actualization tendency, the organismic valuing process and the experiential world.
Trace the development of the self through positive regard, unconditional and conditional positive regard, positive self-regard and conditions of worth.
Explain incongruence, its link to anxiety and defence, and the role of congruence in emotional health.
List and explain each characteristic of the fully functioning person.
Describe Rogers's position on the major questions about human nature and contrast it with Freud's.
Describe person-centred therapy, encounter groups and tests derived from Rogers's ideas as assessment methods.
Explain the Q-sort technique and summarise the research findings on Rogers's theory.
Evaluate Rogers's contributions, criticisms and the reasons for his therapy's rapid acceptance.

sections.heading: The Life of Rogers (1902-1987): Relying on His Own Experience
sections.detailed:
The chapter presents Rogers's early life as the seedbed of his theory. His solitary, self-reliant childhood taught him to trust his own experience above other people's rules, and that conviction later became the centre of person-centred therapy and his idea of the self.

A strict religious home. Rogers was born in 1902 in Oak Park, Illinois, near Chicago, the fourth of six children. His parents held rigid fundamentalist religious views. They stressed moral conduct and hard work and discouraged any display of emotion. The children understood that dancing, card games, movies, smoking, drinking and any sign of sexual interest were forbidden. Rogers later described these teachings as holding him tightly through childhood and adolescence, forcing him to see the world through his parents' eyes rather than his own. Interestingly, his parents exerted their influence in quiet, loving ways, much as Rogers himself later guided clients non-directively. Their beliefs became something he would rebel against.

An older brother and loneliness. Rogers had almost no social life outside the family and believed his parents preferred an older brother, which created strong rivalry. He saw himself as shy, solitary and dreamy, often lost in fantasy. His biographer Milton notes that he grew up remembering being the target of his brother's jokes and receiving little joy from his mother. To escape loneliness he read constantly, even dictionaries and encyclopaedias. This solitude made him depend on his own resources and his personal view of the world, a trait that stayed with him for life and became the foundation of his theory. Rogers himself later said that his interest in interviewing and therapy grew out of this early loneliness, because therapy offered a socially approved way of getting close to people and satisfying a hunger for closeness.

Moths, science and bizarre fantasies. When he was 12 the family moved to a farm about 30 miles from Chicago. Rural life sparked his interest in science: he found, caught and bred a species of moth for months, and he became interested in farming, which his father ran scientifically. Reading about agricultural experiments taught him the value of control groups, isolating a variable and statistical analysis, an unusual interest for a teenager. Yet his emotional life remained troubled. He admitted his fantasies in this period were strange enough that a diagnostician might have called them schizoid.

Freedom in China. Rogers began studying agriculture at the University of Wisconsin, where his parents and several siblings had studied, but after his second year he switched to preparing for the ministry. In his third year he was chosen to attend an international Christian student conference in Beijing. During six months of travel he wrote home that his philosophy was changing: his religious views moved from fundamentalist to liberal. Breaking from his parents' outlook hurt them but gave him emotional and intellectual independence; he realised he could think his own thoughts and reach his own conclusions. This strengthened his belief that every person must learn to rely on their own experiences, ideas and beliefs. The independence was costly: he was hospitalised for five weeks with ulcers, possibly stress-related, and spent a year recovering on the family farm before returning to college.
sections.simple: Rogers grew up in a strict, religious, emotionally restrained family, felt lonely and less favoured than his brother, and escaped into books and fantasy. This forced him to rely on his own experience. A trip to China freed him from his parents' views, convincing him that people should trust their own experience, which became the base of his theory.
keyPoints: Born 1902, Oak Park, Illinois; fourth of six children; fundamentalist, emotion-suppressing parents
Lonely, shy childhood and rivalry with a favoured older brother; Rogers linked his interest in therapy to this loneliness
Farm life at 12 awakened interest in science (moths, scientific agriculture, control groups, statistics)
Trip to Beijing for a Christian student conference shifted his views from fundamentalist to liberal and gave him independence
Lesson he drew: people must rely on their own experiences, ideas and beliefs; the price was a stress-linked ulcer

sections.heading: A Unique Approach to Counseling
sections.detailed:
Training and early work. Rogers graduated from Wisconsin in 1924, married a childhood friend and entered Union Theological Seminary in New York to become a clergyman. After two years he moved across the street to Teachers College, Columbia University, to study clinical and educational psychology, earning his Ph.D. in 1931. He then joined the Child Study Department of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children in Rochester, New York, diagnosing and treating delinquent and underprivileged children.

Academic career. In 1940 he became professor of psychology at Ohio State University, where he began shaping his person-centred approach to counselling emotionally disturbed people and worked to bring clinical psychology into mainstream psychology. From 1945 to 1957 he was at the University of Chicago, teaching and building its Counseling Center.

Breakdown and personal therapy. While in Chicago, he was unable to help a severely disturbed client and became so distressed that he suffered what was then called a nervous breakdown. His confidence collapsed; he felt worthless as a person and inadequate as a therapist, with no future in psychology. He and his wife withdrew to their cabin in upstate New York for six months. On returning he entered therapy himself and discovered how deep his insecurity ran: he had believed nobody could truly love him, even if they liked what he did. The therapy appears to have worked; he came out able to give and receive love and to form deep emotional bonds, including with clients.

How his clients differed from Freud's. From 1957 to 1963 he taught at the University of Wisconsin and published widely, spreading his theory and therapy. His clinical work in academia was mostly with college students in counselling centres: young, intelligent, very verbal people facing adjustment problems rather than severe emotional disorders. This population was very different from the patients seen by Freudians or private-practice clinicians, which helps explain the optimistic, conscious, present-focused flavour of his theory.

Later life and honours. In 1964 he became a resident fellow at the Western Behavioral Sciences Institute in California and applied his person-centred philosophy to international conflicts, such as tension between Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland and between Jews and Arabs in the Middle East. He was president of the American Psychological Association in 1946 and received both its Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award and Distinguished Professional Contribution Award.
sections.simple: Rogers moved from training for the church to studying psychology, worked with troubled children, then taught at several universities. After a breakdown and his own therapy he learned to give and receive love. His clients were mostly bright, verbal students with everyday adjustment problems, unlike Freud's seriously disturbed patients.
keyPoints: Ph.D. from Teachers College, Columbia (1931); worked with delinquent and underprivileged children in Rochester
Ohio State (1940): began forming person-centred ideas; Chicago (1945-1957): built the Counseling Center
Breakdown after failing a disturbed client; personal therapy revealed deep insecurity and freed him to form close bonds
Clients were young, intelligent, verbal students with adjustment problems, unlike Freud's patients
APA president 1946; later applied his ideas to international conflict (Northern Ireland, Middle East)

sections.heading: The Self and the Tendency toward Actualization: Self-Insight
sections.detailed:
Rogers's China trip taught him how important an autonomous self had been in his own growth, and his early research pushed him further toward the self as the centre of personality.

Rating children in the 1930s. Rogers devised a method for judging whether a child's behaviour was healthy and constructive or unhealthy and destructive. He studied each child's background and had the child rated on factors he thought would shape behaviour: family environment, health, intellectual development, economic circumstances, cultural influences, social interactions and level of education. All of these are external, belonging to the child's environment. He also looked at one internal factor, self-insight or self-understanding, which he defined as accepting oneself and reality and taking responsibility for oneself. At this stage he still believed the external factors mattered more.

Kell's study. About ten years later William Kell, one of Rogers's students, tried to predict the behaviour of delinquent children. Rogers expected family environment and social interactions to correlate most strongly with delinquency. He was wrong: self-insight was the best predictor of later behaviour. Rogers admitted he could not accept the result and shelved the study.

McNeil's replication. Two years later Helen McNeil repeated the study with a different group of children and obtained similar results: the person's level of self-insight was the single most important predictor of behaviour. Faced with this accumulating evidence, Rogers accepted the finding and saw its significance.

Implications. If a person's attitude toward the self predicts behaviour better than the external childhood factors everyone assumed were crucial, then counsellors and social workers had been emphasising the wrong things. Traditionally they changed the external situation, for example by removing a child from a threatening home and placing him or her in foster care. Rogers concluded they should instead try to change the child's self-insight. This persuaded him to devote his career to a therapy that builds self-understanding, self-direction and personal responsibility rather than changes in the social environment, and to focus on studying the self and how it changes. The self thus became the core of his theory, just as it had become the core of his own life.
sections.simple: Rogers first thought outside factors like family and money shaped children's behaviour most. Studies by his students Kell and McNeil showed instead that a child's self-insight best predicted later delinquent behaviour. This convinced Rogers to build his therapy and theory around the self.
keyPoints: 1930s: Rogers rated children on external factors (family, health, intellect, economics, culture, social life, education) plus self-insight
Self-insight = accepting self and reality plus responsibility for oneself
Kell's study: self-insight, not family environment, best predicted delinquent behaviour; Rogers shelved it
McNeil replicated the result two years later, and Rogers accepted it
Conclusion: counsellors should change self-insight, not just the environment; the self became the core of his theory

sections.heading: Actualizing Tendency
sections.detailed:
Rogers held that people have one innate, basic motive: a tendency to actualize, maintain and enhance the self. The drive toward self-actualization is one part of a broader actualization tendency that covers all our physiological and psychological needs.

Maintaining the organism. By meeting basic needs such as food, water and safety, the actualization tendency keeps the organism alive, providing for sustenance and survival.

Biological growth. Rogers believed the tendency starts in the womb. It promotes growth by guiding the differentiation of physical organs and the development of physiological functions. It is responsible for maturation, the genetically determined development of the body's parts and processes, from the growth of the foetus to the appearance of secondary sex characteristics at puberty. These changes are programmed in our genes but are brought to completion by the actualization tendency.

Growth involves struggle. Although such changes are genetically set, progress toward full human development is neither automatic nor easy; it involves struggle and pain. Rogers's example is a child learning to walk: the child falls, gets hurt and cries, and staying at the crawling stage would be less painful, yet most children keep trying. They persist because the tendency to actualize is stronger than any urge to regress just because growth is hard.

Psychological growth. Beyond the body, the same tendency drives the development of our abilities and potentials to the fullest, with the ultimate goal of actualizing the self and becoming a fully functioning person. Rogers proposed this as the single overriding motivation in his theory.
sections.simple: Rogers said humans have one inborn motive: to grow, maintain and improve themselves. This actualization tendency keeps us alive, guides bodily maturation from the womb to puberty, and pushes psychological growth. Growth is not easy, but the urge to grow beats the urge to go back, as with a toddler who keeps trying to walk.
keyPoints: Single innate motive: to actualize, maintain and enhance the self
Self-actualization is part of a wider actualization tendency covering physiological and psychological needs
Maintains the organism by meeting needs for food, water, safety
Begins in the womb; drives maturation (organ differentiation to secondary sex characteristics)
Growth involves struggle and pain, but the actualizing urge is stronger than the urge to regress (learning to walk)

sections.heading: Organismic Valuing Process
sections.detailed:
For Rogers the process that governs behaviour throughout life is the organismic valuing process. Through it we judge every experience by how well it serves the actualization tendency.

Experiences we perceive as helping actualization are judged good and desirable and given a positive value. Experiences perceived as blocking actualization are judged undesirable and given a negative value.

These evaluations shape behaviour because we prefer to repeat desirable experiences and avoid undesirable ones. In this way the organismic valuing process acts as an inner compass, steering a person toward what promotes growth.

The chapter later notes that there is some research evidence supporting the concept (page 285). The process becomes important in understanding what goes wrong in development: when children start valuing experiences by whether they win approval from others instead of by whether they serve actualization, incongruence arises.
sections.simple: The organismic valuing process is our inner judge. We rate each experience as good if it helps us grow and bad if it holds us back, and then we seek out the good ones and avoid the bad ones.
keyPoints: Governing process across the whole life span
Evaluates experiences by how well they serve the actualization tendency
Growth-promoting experiences get positive value; hindering ones get negative value
We repeat desirable and avoid undesirable experiences, so it guides behaviour
Some research supports the concept

sections.heading: The Experiential World
sections.detailed:
Rogers considered the experiential world, the everyday world of experience we live in, as a frame of reference or context that influences our growth. Every day we face countless stimuli: some trivial, some important, some threatening, some rewarding. Rogers asked how we perceive and respond to this many-sided world.

Reality is perceived reality. His answer was that the reality of our environment depends on how we perceive it, and our perception may not match objective reality. Two people can react very differently to the same experience; a student may judge a roommate's behaviour very differently from someone decades older. This is why Rogers is described as taking a phenomenological approach: personality can be understood only from the person's own viewpoint, based on subjective experience (the experiential field).

Change with age and circumstance. Our perceptions change over time and with circumstances. What a college student thinks is acceptable behaviour will probably look different by the time he or she is 70.

Broadening in infancy. As the actualization tendency makes infants grow, their experiential world widens. They are exposed to more and more stimulation and respond to it as they subjectively perceive it. Experience becomes the only basis for judgement and behaviour; Rogers called experience his highest authority and the touchstone of validity. Higher levels of development sharpen the experiential world and eventually lead to the development of the self.
sections.simple: Rogers said we each live in our own experiential world: what counts as real is what we perceive, which may not match objective reality. This field of experience grows wider as infants develop, changes as we age, and eventually gives rise to the self.
keyPoints: Experiential world = context or frame of reference that influences growth
Reality depends on our perception, which may differ from objective reality (phenomenological view)
Perceptions differ between people and change with time and age
In infancy the experiential world broadens as the actualization tendency drives growth
Experience is the highest authority; development of the experiential field leads to the self

sections.heading: The Development of the Self in Childhood
sections.detailed:
As infants' social encounters widen and their experiential field becomes more complex, one part of their experience separates from the rest. This part, referred to with the words I, me and myself, is the self or self-concept.

Forming the self-concept involves telling apart what directly belongs to the self from the people, objects and events outside it. The self-concept is also our picture of what we are, what we should be and what we would like to be, which anticipates the later distinction between the perceived self and the ideal self.

Consistency. Ideally the self is a consistent pattern, an organised whole, and all its aspects strive for consistency. For instance, people who are troubled by their aggressive feelings and deny them will not dare to behave in openly aggressive ways, because that would clash with their self-concept, which says they should not be aggressive.

The rest of the developmental account (positive regard, unconditional and conditional positive regard, positive self-regard, conditions of worth and incongruence) explains how this emerging self is shaped by the reactions of other people, especially the mother.
sections.simple: As babies' experiences grow, they begin to separate an 'I' or 'me' from everything else. This self-concept includes who we are, who we should be and who we want to be, and it tries to stay consistent.
keyPoints: Self or self-concept emerges as part of the experiential field becomes differentiated
Refers to I, me, myself; separates what is self from external people, objects, events
Includes what we are, should be, and would like to be
Self strives to be a consistent, organised whole
Behaviour inconsistent with the self-concept is avoided (denied aggression example)

sections.heading: Positive Regard (Unconditional Positive Regard and Positive Self-Regard)
sections.detailed:
Need for positive regard. As the self emerges, infants develop a need for positive regard: acceptance, love and approval from others, especially the mother in infancy. Rogers thought this need is probably learned but said its origin did not matter. It is universal and persistent.

Why it matters. Infants find positive regard satisfying and feel frustrated when it is absent or withdrawn. Because it is crucial to personality development, infant behaviour is guided by the amount of affection and love received. If the mother does not provide positive regard, the infant's innate tendency toward actualization and the development of the self-concept will be hampered. Infants take parental disapproval of their behaviour as disapproval of their developing self. If this happens often, they stop striving for actualization and instead act in ways that win positive regard, even when those actions are inconsistent with their self-concept.

Unconditional positive regard. Even well-loved infants are sometimes punished for specific behaviours. If positive regard continues despite undesirable behaviour, this is unconditional positive regard: the mother's love is given freely and fully and does not depend on the child's behaviour. Rogers saw this as the ideal parental attitude, and in person-centred therapy the therapist offers it to the client.

Reciprocity. The need for positive regard is reciprocal. When we see ourselves satisfying someone else's need for positive regard, our own need is satisfied too, so giving positive regard is rewarding. Because satisfying this need is so important, especially in infancy, we become sensitive to other people's attitudes and behaviour. By interpreting their approval or disapproval we refine our self-concept; in other words, we internalise the attitudes of others.

Positive self-regard. Over time positive regard comes more from within than from others, a condition Rogers called positive self-regard. It becomes as strong as the need for regard from others and can be satisfied the same way. A child rewarded with affection and approval for being happy will come to feel positive self-regard whenever behaving happily; in effect we learn to reward ourselves. Positive self-regard can be described as contentment with oneself and is related to positive mental health (Leising and colleagues, 2013). It too is reciprocal: people who receive positive regard and develop positive self-regard may in turn give positive regard to others.
sections.simple: Babies need love, acceptance and approval from others, especially the mother. When that love is given no matter how the child behaves, it is unconditional positive regard. Over time the child learns to give this approval to itself, which Rogers called positive self-regard.
keyPoints: Positive regard = acceptance, love and approval from others; universal and persistent need, probably learned
Lack of positive regard hampers actualization; infants then act to win approval even against their self-concept
Unconditional positive regard = love given freely, regardless of behaviour; ideal for parents and therapists
Positive regard is reciprocal; we internalise others' attitudes to refine the self-concept
Positive self-regard = granting ourselves acceptance and approval; linked to positive mental health (Leising et al., 2013)

sections.heading: Conditions of Worth
sections.detailed:
Conditions of worth grow out of the developmental sequence in which positive regard leads to positive self-regard. Rogers treated positive self-regard as his version of Freud's superego, and he said it derives from conditional positive regard.

Conditional positive regard. This is the opposite of unconditional positive regard. Parents do not respond to everything an infant does with approval. Some behaviours annoy, frighten or bore them, and for those they withhold affection. The infant learns that parental affection has a price: it depends on behaving in acceptable ways. The child learns that sometimes it is prized and sometimes not.

Internalising external standards. If a parent shows annoyance every time the infant drops something out of the crib, the child learns to disapprove of himself or herself for that behaviour. External standards become internal and personal; children come to punish themselves as their parents did. They develop self-regard only in situations that earned parental approval, and the self-concept formed this way works as a stand-in parent.

Conditions of worth. The result is conditions of worth: the belief that one is worthy only under certain conditions, namely those that brought parental positive regard and then personal positive self-regard. Having absorbed their parents' norms, children judge themselves as worthy or unworthy, good or bad, in the parents' terms. This is why the concept is compared to the superego: both are internalised parental standards that judge the self, though in Rogers's account they arise from conditional love and approval rather than from resolution of psychosexual conflict.

Research example. A study of adolescents found that when mothers used conditional regard (the text says conditional positive self-regard) to reward academic achievement and punish non-achievement, the adolescents' self-worth became unstable. With good grades they acted in self-aggrandising ways; without them they felt shame and devalued themselves (Assor & Tai, 2012).

Consequences. Children learn to avoid certain behaviours and no longer function freely. Because they must carefully evaluate their behaviours and attitudes and hold back from certain actions, they cannot fully develop or actualize the self. They restrict their growth by living within their conditions of worth.
sections.simple: When parents give love only for 'good' behaviour (conditional positive regard), children learn they are worthy only under certain conditions. They absorb these rules, judge themselves by them like a Freudian superego, and stop acting freely, which blocks their growth.
keyPoints: Conditional positive regard = approval given only for desirable behaviours and attitudes
Infants learn parental affection has a price; external standards become internal
Conditions of worth = feeling worthy only when behaving in approved ways; similar to Freud's superego
Self-concept formed this way acts as a parental surrogate; children punish themselves as parents did
Assor & Tai (2012): mothers' conditional regard for grades made adolescents' self-worth erratic
Living within conditions of worth inhibits actualization

sections.heading: Incongruence
sections.detailed:
Children not only learn to hold back unacceptable behaviours; they may also deny or distort unacceptable ways of perceiving their experiential world. By holding inaccurate perceptions of certain experiences they risk becoming estranged from their true self.

The root problem is a shift in how experiences are evaluated. Instead of judging experiences by how they contribute to the actualization tendency (the organismic valuing process), we judge them by whether they bring positive regard from others. This produces incongruence: a discrepancy between the self-concept and the experiential world, the environment as we perceive it.

Incongruence and anxiety. Experiences that are incompatible with the self-concept become threatening and show up as anxiety. Rogers's example: if my self-concept says I love all of humanity, then meeting someone I hate will make me anxious, because hating does not fit my image of myself as a loving person.

Defence. To protect the self-concept, I must deny the hatred. We defend against the anxiety that comes with the threat by distorting the experience, which shuts off part of our experiential field. The result is rigidity in some of our perceptions. Later research (page 287) links incongruence between perceived self and ideal self with poor emotional adjustment.
sections.simple: Incongruence is a mismatch between how we see ourselves and what we actually experience. When an experience does not fit our self-image, we feel anxious and deny or distort it, which makes our perceptions rigid and cuts us off from our true self.
keyPoints: Children may deny or distort perceptions that conflict with conditions of worth
Experiences are judged by whether they win approval, not by whether they aid actualization
Incongruence = discrepancy between self-concept and experience
Incongruent experiences are threatening and produce anxiety (hating someone vs. loving all humanity)
Defence by denial and distortion closes off part of the experiential field and makes perceptions rigid

sections.heading: Congruence and Emotional Health
sections.detailed:
Rogers held that psychological adjustment and emotional health depend on the degree of congruence, or compatibility, between the self-concept and experience.

Psychologically healthy people perceive themselves, others and events largely as they really are. They are open to new experiences because nothing threatens their self-concept, and they have no need to deny or distort perceptions. The reason is developmental: as children they received unconditional positive regard and did not have to internalise conditions of worth.

Such people feel worthy in all conditions and situations and can use all their experiences. They can develop and actualize every aspect of the self, moving toward becoming a fully functioning person and living what Rogers called the good life.

This section links the developmental account to the description of the fully functioning person: unconditional positive regard leads to no conditions of worth, which leads to congruence, openness and full functioning.
sections.simple: Emotional health means our self-concept fits our experience. People who were loved unconditionally as children have no conditions of worth, so nothing threatens them; they see reality accurately, stay open to experience, and move toward the 'good life'.
keyPoints: Adjustment depends on congruence between self-concept and experience
Healthy people perceive self, others and events realistically
They are open to experience and need no denial or distortion
Cause: unconditional positive regard in childhood, so no conditions of worth
They feel worthy in all situations and move toward full functioning and 'the good life'

sections.heading: Characteristics of Fully Functioning Persons
sections.detailed:
For Rogers the fully functioning person is the most desirable outcome of psychological development and social evolution. Fully functioning is his term for self-actualization, the development of all facets of the self. He described several characteristics (summarised in Table 10.1).

1. Awareness of all experience. Fully functioning persons do not distort or deny any experience; all of it reaches the self. There is no defensiveness because nothing threatens the self-concept. They are open to positive feelings such as courage and tenderness and to negative ones such as fear and pain. They are more emotional in the sense of accepting a wider range of emotions and feeling them more intensely.

2. Living fully in every moment (freshness of appreciation). Every experience is potentially fresh and new. Experiences cannot be predicted in advance; they are lived and participated in fully rather than merely watched.

3. Trust in one's own organism. They trust their own reactions rather than being guided by others' opinions, a social code or purely intellectual judgement. Doing what feels right is a good guide to doing what is satisfying. Rogers did not mean they ignore their intellect or other people; rather, all information is accepted as congruent with the self-concept. Since nothing is threatening, all data can be perceived and weighed accurately, and decisions come from considering all experiential data. Because self and experience are congruent, they are unaware of this weighing, so their decisions look more intuitive and emotional than intellectual. This clarifies the role of the intellect: it is one source of data among many, integrated rather than dominant.

4. Freedom of choice without inhibitions. They feel free to choose without constraint, which gives them a sense of personal power. They know their future depends on their own actions, not on present circumstances, past events or other people, and they do not feel forced, by themselves or others, to behave in only one way.

5. Creativity and spontaneity. They live creatively, constructively and adaptively as conditions change. Spontaneity goes with creativity. They are flexible, seek new experiences and challenges, and do not need predictability, security or freedom from tension.

6. In a state of actualizing. Rogers chose the word actualizing, not actualized, because actualized implies a finished, static personality. Self-development is always in progress; being fully functioning is, in his phrase, a direction rather than a destination. If striving and growth stop, the person loses spontaneity, flexibility and openness. The emphasis on change is captured by the word becoming in his book title On Becoming a Person (1961). Table 10.1 also lists a continual need to grow and to maximise one's potential. So a fully functioning person cannot strictly be called self-actualized; he or she is always self-actualizing.

7. Not always easy. Being fully functioning means constantly testing, growing, striving and using all one's potential, a complex and challenging way of life. Rogers did not describe such people as happy, blissful or contented, though they may sometimes be; their lives are better described as enriching, exciting and meaningful.
sections.simple: Fully functioning people are open to all their feelings, live each moment freshly, trust their own reactions, feel free to choose, and are creative and spontaneous. They are always 'actualizing', never finished, and their life is rich and meaningful rather than simply happy.
keyPoints: Aware of all experience; open to both positive and negative feelings, felt intensely
Live fully in each moment; experiences fresh and not predicted
Trust their own organism; intellect and others' views are integrated data, decisions look intuitive
Free choice without inhibition gives a sense of personal power
Creative, spontaneous, flexible; do not need security or predictability
'Actualizing' not 'actualized': a direction, not a destination; the life is challenging, not just happy

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Free will versus determinism. Rogers clearly favoured free will. Fully functioning persons freely create their selves; no part of personality is predetermined.

Nature versus nurture. He gave the environment more weight. The actualization tendency is innate, but the actualizing process itself is shaped more by social than by biological forces.

Past versus present. Childhood experiences have some effect on personality, but later experiences matter more. Present feelings are more vital to personality than childhood events. This is a sharp contrast with Freud, who saw the first five years as decisive.

Uniqueness versus universality. Rogers saw some universality, since fully functioning persons share certain characteristics, but his writings suggest there is room for uniqueness in how those characteristics are expressed.

Goal of life. The ultimate and necessary goal is to become a fully functioning person.

Optimism. A theorist who credits people with the ability, motivation and responsibility to understand and improve themselves clearly takes an optimistic view. Rogers believed we have a basically healthy nature and an innate tendency to grow and fulfil our potential, and he never lost this optimism; at 85 he said that his work with individuals and groups kept reinforcing his positive view of human nature. In his view we are not doomed to conflict with ourselves or society, not ruled by instinctive biological forces, and not controlled by the events of our first five years. Our outlook is progressive rather than regressive, toward growth rather than stagnation. We experience the world openly rather than defensively and seek challenge rather than familiar security. Emotional disturbances may occur but are uncommon.

Therapy and society. Through person-centred therapy people overcome difficulties by drawing on their inner resources, the innate drive for actualization. Rogers admitted that, out of defensiveness and fear, people can act in cruel, destructive, immature and antisocial ways, yet he found strongly positive directional tendencies in such people, as in everyone. The urge to become fully functioning also benefits society: as more people in a culture become self-actualizing, society will naturally improve.

Contrast with Freud. Freud stressed unconscious forces, biological instincts, the decisive role of early childhood and inevitable conflict, giving a pessimistic image. Rogers stressed conscious, rational choice, the present, environmental influence and growth, giving an optimistic and humanistic image.
sections.simple: Rogers believed in free will, gave more weight to environment than biology, and thought present feelings matter more than childhood. He saw people as basically healthy and growth-oriented, so his view of human nature was strongly optimistic, the opposite of Freud's.
keyPoints: Free will: fully functioning people create their selves
Nurture: actualizing process shaped more by social than biological forces
Later experiences and present feelings outweigh childhood events
Some universality (shared traits of fully functioning people) with room for uniqueness in expression
Optimistic: basically healthy nature, growth over stagnation; disturbances uncommon
Self-actualizing individuals lead to a better society

sections.heading: Assessment in Rogers's Theory: Person-Centered Therapy
sections.detailed:
For Rogers the only valid way to assess personality is through the person's subjective experiences: life events as the person perceives them and accepts them as real. He called the people he worked with clients, never patients, and believed they could examine the roots of their problems and redirect personality growth that had been blocked by incongruence between self-concept and experience.

Why the name. The approach was first called non-directive, then client-centred, and finally person-centred therapy. The name signals that the capacity to change and improve personality lies within the person; the person, not the therapist, directs change, and the therapist facilitates it. In person-centred therapy the client is assumed to be responsible for changing his or her own personality.

How it works. Rogers explored the client's feelings and attitudes toward the self and others. He listened without preconceptions, trying to understand the client's experiential world as the client saw it. The therapist's only predetermined belief is the client's inherent value and worth. Clients are accepted as they are: the therapist offers unconditional positive regard, makes no judgements about their behaviour and gives no advice on how to behave. Everything centres on the client, including responsibility for changing behaviour and re-evaluating relationships.

Limitations Rogers acknowledged. He considered it the only worthwhile assessment approach but not infallible. By focusing on subjective experience, the therapist learns only what the client consciously expresses; experiences outside awareness stay hidden. Trying to infer too much about non-conscious material risks reflecting the therapist's own projections rather than the client's experience. Also, what the therapist learns depends on the client's ability to communicate, and since all communication is imperfect, the therapist sees the client's world imperfectly and incompletely.

Advantages claimed. Within these limits Rogers argued that person-centred therapy gives a clearer view of a person's experiential world than any other form of assessment or therapy. It does not rely on a predetermined theoretical framework, like Freudian psychoanalysis, into which the client's problem must be fitted.

Rejection of psychoanalytic techniques. Rogers opposed free association, dream analysis and case histories. He believed they made clients dependent on the therapist, who took on an aura of expertise and authority. They removed personal responsibility by suggesting the therapist knew all about the client, so the client might conclude the expert would solve the problems while he or she simply followed instructions. This is the key difference from the psychoanalytic clinical interview, in which the analyst interprets unconscious material and directs the process.
sections.simple: Rogers assessed personality only through clients' own conscious experience. In person-centred therapy the therapist listens without judging, gives unconditional positive regard and no advice, and the client takes responsibility for change. He rejected free association, dream analysis and case histories because they make clients dependent on an 'expert'.

sections.heading: Encounter Groups
sections.detailed:
Rogers showed that person-centred therapy could help individuals who were out of touch with their feelings and closed to experience. Wanting to bring this enhanced psychological health to more people, he developed a group technique, the encounter group (Rogers, 1970), in which people learn about themselves and about how they relate to, or encounter, one another.

Format. Groups had 8 to 15 members and typically met for 20 to 60 hours over several sessions. They began with no formal structure or agenda. Group facilitators were not leaders in the usual sense; they created an atmosphere in which members could express themselves and focus on how others saw them. The facilitator's job was to make it easier for members to gain self-insight and become more fully functioning. Rogers believed most, though not all, participants would become more fully functioning.

Evidence. Not all psychologists agreed. A large-scale analysis of studies (Faith, Wong, & Carpenter, 1995) found encounter group results comparable to traditional psychotherapies. It also found that larger groups meeting more often produced better outcomes than smaller groups meeting less often.

Today. Encounter groups are less popular than when Rogers promoted them, but some of his followers still run them to help people enhance their potential and become more fully functioning.
sections.simple: Encounter groups were Rogers's group version of his therapy. Eight to fifteen people met for many hours with no agenda, and a facilitator helped them gain self-insight by seeing how others perceived them. Research found results similar to traditional therapy, with bigger, more frequent groups doing better.

sections.heading: Psychological Tests
sections.detailed:
Rogers did not use psychological tests to assess personality and did not create any. Other psychologists, however, built tests to measure aspects of the experiential world.

The Experience Inventory (Coan, 1972) is a self-report questionnaire that tries to assess openness or receptivity to experience, a characteristic of the fully functioning person.

The Experiencing Scale (Gendlin & Tomlinson, 1967) measures level of self-trust. People being assessed do not answer items directly; they talk about whatever they like, and their recorded comments are later rated for self-trust, for example how far they treat their feelings as an important source of information for behaviour, or how far they deny that feelings influence their decisions.

Research use. The Experiencing Scale has been used with person-centred therapy. One study (Klein, Malthieu, Gendlin, & Kiesler, 1969) found that clients who improved most in therapy showed an increase in self-trust from before to after therapy, while those who improved little showed small or no increases. People with less severe emotional disorders showed more self-trust than those with more severe disorders.
sections.simple: Rogers did not use tests, but others made some. The Experience Inventory measures openness to experience, and the Experiencing Scale rates self-trust from people's free talk. Clients who improved most in therapy showed the biggest rise in self-trust.
keyPoints: Rogers neither used nor developed psychological tests

sections.heading: Research on Rogers's Theory
sections.detailed:
Rogers's view of research. Rogers believed person-centred interviews, relying on clients' self-reports, were more valuable than experimental methods; orthodox scientific approaches, in his view, revealed less about personality than his clinical approach. He once said he never learned anything from research and that most of his research only confirmed what he already felt to be true (quoted in Bergin & Strupp, 1972).

Using research to verify. Although he did not collect personality data in laboratories, he did use research methods to try to confirm his clinical observations. He was enthusiastic about studying what happens in therapy sessions, an idea many clinicians resisted as a violation of privacy.

Recording therapy sessions. Rogers introduced a procedure that was radical at the time (Goldfried, 2007): he recorded and filmed therapy sessions so researchers could study the client-therapist interaction. Before this, the only data were the therapist's after-the-fact notes written some time after the session. Such notes suffer from memory distortion and miss the client's emotional state and body language, though a facial expression or tone of voice can reveal more than words. With recordings everything became available for study. Rogers called the method a microscope for examining the molecules of personality change. He always obtained clients' permission and found the equipment did not interfere with therapy.
sections.simple: Rogers trusted clients' self-reports more than experiments, but he still used research to check his ideas. His big innovation was recording and filming therapy sessions, so researchers could study what actually happens between client and therapist instead of relying on the therapist's later notes.
keyPoints: Rogers valued person-centred interviews and self-reports over experimental methods
Used research to verify clinical observations, despite saying he learned nothing from it

sections.heading: Evaluating Person-Centered Therapy
sections.detailed:
Rogers and his associates studied how the self-concept changes during therapy. Despite Rogers's claim that he was not a scientist, they used qualitative and quantitative techniques, applying rating scales and content analyses of clients' verbal statements.

The Q-sort technique. Much of this research used the Q-sort, a procedure developed by William Stephenson (1953). Clients sort a large number of statements about the self-concept into categories ranging from most descriptive to least descriptive of themselves. The Q-sort is thus a way of empirically defining, or quantifying, the client's self-image. Typical items include statements such as enjoying being alone, feeling helpless or being emotionally mature. Clients can sort the statements first for the perceived self and then for the ideal self, the person they would most like to be. Using correlation, Rogers measured how closely the perceived self matched the ideal self, and how much this changed from before to after therapy.

The case of Mrs. Oak. For one client, Mrs. Oak, the initial correlation between perceived and ideal self was +.36. A year after therapy it had risen to +.79, which Rogers took as evidence that her perceived self had become much more congruent with her ideal self and that her emotional health had improved (Rogers, 1954). Before therapy she saw herself as dependent and passive and felt rejected; she described herself with statements such as feeling driven, insecure, disorganised and needing to protect herself with excuses. Twelve months after therapy she felt more like the self she wanted to be: more secure, less fearful, better able to relate to others, expressing emotions freely, self-reliant, adequate and emotionally mature (Table 10.2).

Butler and Haigh (1954). Rogers's associates measured the perceived-ideal discrepancy in 25 clients and found it decreased during and after therapy. The average correlation rose from .01 before therapy to +.31 after.

Therapist qualities. More recent research shows person-centred therapy is more likely to succeed when clients perceive the therapist as (1) empathic and understanding, (2) showing unconditional positive regard and (3) congruent, that is, genuine in the relationship (Cain, 2013).

Sexual Satisfaction Q-Sort. A newer Q-sort has people sort 63 statements about their behaviours, feelings and experiences during sexual satisfaction. Initial findings suggest most people sort their experiences into one or more of four categories: emotional and masculine, relational and feminine, partner focused, or orgasm focused (McClelland, 2014a, 2014b).

Conditional positive regard. Research on three generations of women and on college students showed that parents' use of conditional positive regard did produce the behaviours they wanted. However, children of such parents reported poor coping skills, fluctuating self-esteem, low self-worth, feelings of parental disapproval and resentment toward their parents. Children whose parents did not use conditional regard reported none of these negative effects (Assor, Roth, & Deci, 2004).

Organismic valuing process and culture. There is some evidence supporting the organismic valuing process. Studies also suggest positive self-regard may be less prevalent in a collectivist culture such as Japan than in an individualistic culture such as the United States (Heine, Lehman, Markus, & Kitayama, 1999; Joseph & Linley, 2005; Sheldon, Arndt, & Houser-Marko, 2003).
sections.simple: Rogers's team used the Q-sort, where clients sort self-statements from most to least like them, to compare perceived and ideal selves. After therapy the two became much closer, as in the case of Mrs. Oak (+.36 to +.79). Other research shows therapy works best with empathic, accepting, genuine therapists, and that conditional parental love has harmful effects.

sections.heading: Openness to Experience
sections.detailed:
In a classic study, Chodorkoff (1954) tested Rogers's proposition that fully functioning persons are open to all experiences, while psychologically unhealthy people build defences against experiences that threaten their self-image.

Method. College students completed a Q-sort self-description. Clinicians prepared a separate Q-sort description of each student based on several sources, including the Thematic Apperception Test and the Rorschach inkblot test. On the basis of these clinical measures the students were divided into good-adjustment and poor-adjustment groups. Perceptual defence was measured by how quickly students recognised neutral words such as table versus supposedly threatening words such as penis.

Results. All students were slower to perceive threatening words than neutral ones, but this delay was more marked among the defensive, poorly adjusted students. The well-adjusted, presumably healthier group showed significantly less perceptual defence. Also, the closer the agreement between a student's self-description and the clinicians' description, the better adjusted the student was.

Meaning. The findings support Rogers's ideas that healthy people are open rather than defensive and that good adjustment involves perceiving oneself accurately, so that self-descriptions match descriptions made by others.
sections.simple: Chodorkoff tested whether healthy people are more open to experience. All students were slower to recognise threatening words, but poorly adjusted students were much slower, showing more defence. Better-adjusted students also described themselves more like clinicians described them.
keyPoints: Chodorkoff (1954) tested openness vs. defensiveness
Self Q-sorts compared with clinicians' Q-sorts based on TAT and Rorschach
Perceptual defence measured with neutral vs. threatening words
Poorly adjusted students showed more perceptual defence
Closer self-clinician agreement = better adjustment

sections.heading: Acceptance of Self
sections.detailed:
Mothers' self-acceptance. Medinnus and Curtis (1963) studied 56 mothers, based on Rogers's idea that people who accept their own nature realistically, whose perceived and ideal selves are congruent, are more likely to accept others as they are. Self-accepting mothers were significantly more accepting of their children's nature than mothers who were not self-accepting, and a child's self-acceptance depended partly on the mother's self-acceptance.

Racial identity. A study of multiracial adults in the United States found that people with high self-acceptance of their racial identities showed stronger positive growth than those with less self-acceptance (Pedrotti & Edwards, 2010).

Parental behaviour. Parents who accepted their children unconditionally and used democratic child-rearing had children with higher self-esteem and greater emotional security than parents who did not accept their children and behaved in an authoritarian way (Baldwin, 1949). Parents of children with high self-esteem showed affection and used reward rather than punishment, while parents of low-self-esteem children were more aloof, less loving and more punitive (Coopersmith, 1967). Adolescents whose parents gave unconditional positive regard and let them express themselves freely developed greater creative potential (Harrington, Block, & Block, 1987).

Unconditional versus conditional regard in adolescence. Adolescents who received unconditional positive regard from parents were more confident and hopeful about getting support from others in future and acted more in line with their perceived interests and talents. Teens who received conditional regard lacked this confidence and hope and acted more often against their true selves to win parental approval (Harter, Marold, Whitesell, & Cobbs, 1996). High school students who received unconditional positive regard from teachers scored higher in positive self-esteem (Nolan, 2008).

Age. Growing older has been found to increase self-adjustment and decrease anger and anxiety (Shallcross, Ford, Floerke, & Mauss, 2013).
sections.simple: Studies show that self-accepting people accept others more: self-accepting mothers accepted their children more, and children's self-acceptance partly mirrored their mothers'. Children and teens given unconditional acceptance by parents or teachers had higher self-esteem, security, creativity and confidence; conditional regard pushed teens to act against their true selves.

sections.heading: Emotional Adjustment
sections.detailed:
Several studies support Rogers's idea that incongruence between perceived self and ideal self signals poor emotional adjustment. The greater the discrepancy, the higher the anxiety, insecurity, self-doubt, depression, social incompetence and other psychological disorders.

High inconsistency between perceived and ideal self also correlates with low self-actualization and low self-esteem (Achenbach & Zigler, 1963; Gough, Fioravanti, & Lazzari, 1983; Mahoney & Hartnett, 1973; Moretti & Higgins, 1990; Straumann, Vookles, Berenstein, Chaiken, & Higgins, 1991). People with a large discrepancy were rated by others as awkward, confused and unfriendly (Gough, Lazzari, & Fioravanti, 1978).

Unrealised potential. Rogers believed failing to realise the innate actualization tendency leads to maladjustment. Ford (1991) tested this using the inherited temperaments proposed by Buss and Plomin: Emotionality, Activity and Sociability (EAS). College students' parents used the EAS Temperament Survey to recall their children's temperaments when very young, and these profiles were compared with the students' current self-perceptions on the same three temperaments. The greater the gap between childhood potential and adult realisation, the greater the maladjustment, supporting Rogers.

Highlights of the research. The chapter's summary box lists the main findings: positive self-regard may matter more in individualistic cultures; fully functioning persons are open to all experiences; a child's self-acceptance depends partly on the mother's; children accepted unconditionally have high self-esteem; people with perceived-ideal incongruence are poorly adjusted with low self-esteem and self-actualization; and failing to realise our innate potential can lead to maladjustment.
sections.simple: Research backs Rogers: the bigger the gap between how people see themselves and how they want to be, the more anxious, depressed and insecure they are, and the lower their self-esteem. Ford found that students who had drifted further from their childhood temperament potential were more maladjusted.

Discrepancy correlates with low self-actualization and self-esteem (several studies)

sections.heading: Reflections on Rogers's Theory: Criticisms
sections.detailed:
Rogers insisted that personality could be explored only through person-centred therapy, by examining subjective experiences through clients' self-reports.

Critics argue that he therefore ignored factors outside the client's conscious awareness that can still influence behaviour.

A second criticism concerns the reliability of self-reports. People may distort accounts of their subjective experience, repressing some events and elaborating on or inventing others, in order to hide their true nature and present an idealised self-image. Rogers's method accepts such reports at face value, so distortions can go undetected.

The chapter summary restates these two points: the theory is criticised for ignoring unconscious forces and for accepting possibly distorted self-reports. Rogers himself acknowledged related limits of person-centred assessment (page 282).
sections.simple: Critics say Rogers relied only on what clients consciously reported, so he ignored unconscious influences on behaviour. They also note that people may distort, hide or invent experiences in self-reports to look better.
keyPoints: Rogers relied solely on self-reports in person-centred therapy
Criticism 1: ignores factors outside conscious awareness that influence behaviour
Criticism 2: self-reports may be distorted, repressed, elaborated or invented
People may present an idealised self-image

sections.heading: The Influence of World War II on Person-Centered Therapy
sections.detailed:
Person-centred therapy became popular very quickly, partly because of social conditions in the United States at the end of World War II in 1945.

Veterans returning from overseas needed help adjusting to civilian life, creating demand for psychologists and for a counselling technique that could be learned and applied quickly.

Traditional psychoanalysis required a medical degree and long specialisation. Person-centred therapy, as one analyst (DeCarvalho, 1999) put it, was simple, informal and brief and required little training.

More than 400 college counselling centres based on Rogers's ideas were set up after the war under the Veterans Administration to help veterans adjust. Client-centred therapy got an enormous boost, and hundreds more colleges established their own counselling centres.

Rogers later acknowledged that the stresses of post-war America propelled his method and his name to prominence and worldwide fame as a leader of a new approach to understanding and treating personality.
sections.simple: Rogers's therapy caught on fast after World War II because huge numbers of returning veterans needed help and there were not enough trained therapists. His method was simple, brief and easy to learn, unlike psychoanalysis, so hundreds of counselling centres adopted it.
keyPoints: Rapid acceptance helped by post-1945 social conditions

sections.heading: Acceptance of Rogers's Therapy
sections.detailed:
Rogers's therapy is used both to treat emotional disturbance and to enhance self-image.

In business it has been used to train managers. In the helping professions it is used to train clinical psychologists, social workers and counsellors.

Therapists of many different orientations have adopted some of Rogers's core concepts, so the person-centred approach remains influential in counselling and psychotherapy (Bohart, 2014; Hazler, 2011; Kirschenbaum & Jourdan, 2005; Patterson & Joseph, 2007).

More than 200 training centres, mostly in Europe, promote his therapy, and several dozen journals are devoted to research and application of his ideas (Murdock, 2008). The journal Person-Centered & Experiential Psychotherapies began in 2002 and remains influential.
sections.simple: Rogers's therapy is widely used, not just for emotional problems but also to improve self-image, train managers, and train psychologists, social workers and counsellors. Over 200 training centres and dozens of journals keep it alive today.

sections.heading: Rogers's Personality Theory
sections.detailed:
Rogers's personality theory has been less influential than his psychotherapy but has still been widely recognised, especially for its emphasis on the self-concept.

Rogers did not believe he had influenced academic or scientific psychology. Nevertheless, his theory and therapy stimulated research on the nature of psychotherapy, the client-therapist interaction and the self-concept, and his ideas significantly shaped psychology's theoretical and empirical definitions of the self.

His background combined clinic, lecture hall and laboratory. He drew on extensive experience with emotionally disturbed clients and on stimulation from colleagues and students, and he attracted many followers who continue to test his ideas in clinical and laboratory settings.

Overall evaluation. Strengths: emphasis on the self-concept, optimistic view of human growth, innovative recording of therapy, the Q-sort research tradition, and wide practical application. Weaknesses: neglect of unconscious factors and dependence on possibly distorted self-reports.
sections.simple: Rogers's personality theory is less famous than his therapy but is valued for putting the self-concept at the centre. It sparked research on therapy, the client-therapist relationship and the self, and his followers still test his ideas.

studies.title: Leising et al. (2013)

studies.title: Assor & Tai (2012)

studies.title: Faith, Wong, & Carpenter (1995)

studies.title: Klein, Malthieu, Gendlin, & Kiesler (1969)
studies.finding: Clients who improved most in therapy showed increased self-trust on the Experiencing Scale; little improvement went with little or no increase; less severe disorders went with more self-trust.

studies.title: Recording therapy sessions
studies.finding: Rogers's recordings showed the presence of equipment did not impede therapy and made the full client-therapist interaction available for study.

studies.title: Mrs. Oak (Rogers, 1954)
studies.finding: Perceived-ideal self correlation rose from +.36 before to +.79 a year after therapy; she moved from feeling dependent, passive and rejected to secure, less fearful and better able to relate.

studies.title: Butler & Haigh (1954)
studies.finding: In 25 clients, perceived-ideal discrepancy decreased; average correlation rose from .01 before therapy to +.31 after.

studies.title: Cain (2013)
studies.finding: Therapy is more successful when clients see therapists as empathic and understanding, showing unconditional positive regard, and congruent (genuine).

studies.title: McClelland (2014): Sexual Satisfaction Q-Sort
studies.finding: People sorting 63 statements tended to group their experiences into emotional and masculine, relational and feminine, partner focused, or orgasm focused.

studies.title: Assor, Roth, & Deci (2004)
studies.finding: Parents' conditional regard produced desired behaviours but children reported poor coping, fluctuating self-esteem, low self-worth, felt disapproval and resentment; no such effects without conditional regard.

studies.title: Organismic valuing and culture (Heine et al., 1999; Joseph & Linley, 2005; Sheldon et al., 2003)
studies.finding: Some evidence supports the organismic valuing process; positive self-regard may be less prevalent in collectivist Japan than in the individualist US.

studies.title: Chodorkoff (1954)
studies.finding: All students perceived threatening words more slowly, but poorly adjusted students showed more perceptual defence; closer agreement between self and clinician Q-sorts meant better adjustment.

studies.title: Medinnus & Curtis (1963)
studies.finding: Among 56 mothers, self-accepting mothers accepted their children more; a child's self-acceptance partly depended on the mother's.

studies.title: Pedrotti & Edwards (2010)
studies.finding: Multiracial US adults high in self-acceptance of racial identity showed stronger positive growth.

studies.title: Baldwin (1949)
studies.finding: Unconditionally accepting, democratic parents had children with higher self-esteem and emotional security than rejecting, authoritarian parents.

studies.title: Coopersmith (1967)
studies.finding: Parents of high-self-esteem children were affectionate and used reward; parents of low-self-esteem children were aloof, less loving and more punitive.

studies.title: Harrington, Block, & Block (1987)
studies.finding: Adolescents given unconditional positive regard and freedom to express themselves had greater creative potential.

studies.title: Harter, Marold, Whitesell, & Cobbs (1996)
studies.finding: Teens with unconditional parental regard were more confident and hopeful about future support and acted in line with their interests; those with conditional regard acted against their true selves to gain approval.

studies.title: Nolan (2008)
studies.finding: High school students receiving unconditional positive regard from teachers had higher positive self-esteem.

studies.title: Shallcross, Ford, Floerke, & Mauss (2013)
studies.finding: Growing older increases self-adjustment and decreases anger and anxiety.

studies.title: Perceived-ideal discrepancy studies (Achenbach & Zigler, 1963; Gough et al., 1983; Mahoney & Hartnett, 1973; Moretti & Higgins, 1990; Straumann et al., 1991)
studies.finding: Greater discrepancy goes with more anxiety, insecurity, self-doubt, depression and social incompetence, and with low self-actualization and self-esteem.

studies.title: Gough, Lazzari, & Fioravanti (1978)
studies.finding: People with large perceived-ideal discrepancies were rated by others as awkward, confused and unfriendly.

studies.title: Ford (1991)
studies.finding: The greater the gap between parent-recalled childhood EAS temperament and students' current self-perceptions, the greater the maladjustment.
