practice.q: Explain how Rogers's childhood and early life shaped his interest in therapy and his theory of personality. How did his clinical experience differ from Freud's?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Carl Rogers (1902-1987), founder of person-centred therapy, built his theory not from laboratory experiments but from his own life and his work with clients. The chapter shows that his solitary childhood, his break from his parents' beliefs, his personal crisis and the kind of clients he treated all left a clear stamp on his ideas about the self, experience and growth.

A strict, emotionally restrained home. Rogers was born in Oak Park, Illinois, the fourth of six children. His parents held strict fundamentalist religious views, stressed moral behaviour and hard work, and suppressed displays of emotion. Dancing, cards, films, smoking, drinking and any sexual interest were forbidden. Rogers felt these teachings gripped him and made him live by his parents' view of the world rather than his own. His parents influenced him in subtle and loving ways, much as he later influenced clients non-directively, and their beliefs became a target for his revolt.

Loneliness and self-reliance. Rogers had almost no social life outside the family and believed his parents favoured an older brother, with whom he competed and whose jokes he endured. He was shy, dreamy and lost in fantasy, and escaped into constant reading. This isolation forced him to rely on his own resources and his personal view of the world, a trait that became the foundation of his theory, which treats a person's own experience as the highest authority. Rogers himself said his interest in interviewing and therapy grew out of this loneliness: therapy gave him a socially approved way of becoming close to people and satisfying his hunger for closeness.

Science and independence. On the family farm, from age 12, he bred moths and read about scientific agriculture, learning to value control groups, isolating variables and statistics, which later showed in his willingness to test therapy through research. At the University of Wisconsin he moved from agriculture toward the ministry, and a six-month trip to a Christian student conference in Beijing shifted his religious views from fundamentalist to liberal. Freeing himself from his parents gave him emotional and intellectual independence and convinced him that every person must learn to rely on their own experiences, ideas and beliefs, a core idea of person-centred therapy. The cost was a stress-linked ulcer and a year of recovery.

Breakdown and personal therapy. After training at Union Theological Seminary and Teachers College, Columbia, and working with delinquent children in Rochester, Rogers held posts at Ohio State and Chicago. In Chicago, failing to help a severely disturbed client triggered a breakdown and feelings of complete worthlessness. In his own therapy he discovered he believed no one could love him. Successful therapy left him able to give and receive love, a personal experience of the healing power of acceptance that mirrors his later emphasis on unconditional positive regard.

Difference from Freud's clinical experience. Much of Rogers's academic clinical work, especially at Wisconsin (1957-1963), was with college students in counselling centres. These clients were young, intelligent, highly verbal and generally facing adjustment problems rather than severe emotional disorders. They differed sharply from the patients treated by Freudians or private-practice clinicians. This helps explain why Rogers saw people as conscious, rational and growth-oriented, gave little weight to unconscious forces and the past, and regarded emotional disturbance as uncommon.

Conclusion. Rogers's loneliness gave him a hunger for closeness that drew him to therapy; his self-reliance and break from his parents taught him to trust personal experience; his own therapy showed him the power of acceptance; and his bright, mildly troubled student clients encouraged an optimistic, present-focused view. Together these explain why his theory centres on the self, subjective experience and the actualizing tendency rather than on Freud's unconscious conflicts.

practice.q: Describe the research on delinquent children that influenced Rogers's view of the role of the self in personality.
practice.answer:
In the 1930s Rogers developed a way of judging whether a child's behaviour was healthy or destructive. Children were rated on external factors such as family environment, health, intellectual development, economic circumstances, cultural influences, social interactions and education, and on one internal factor, self-insight (acceptance of self and reality and responsibility for oneself). Rogers believed the external factors were more important.

About ten years later his student William Kell tried to predict delinquent children's behaviour. Rogers expected family environment and social interactions to be the strongest predictors, but self-insight predicted later behaviour best. Rogers could not accept this and shelved the study. Two years later Helen McNeil replicated it with different children and again found self-insight to be the single most important predictor.

Rogers then accepted the evidence. He reasoned that counsellors had been focusing on the wrong things by changing children's environments, for example through foster care, when they should be changing self-insight. This led him to develop a therapy that promotes self-understanding, self-direction and responsibility, and made the self the core of his personality theory.

practice.q: Explain how the actualization tendency promotes both biological and psychological growth.
practice.answer:
Rogers proposed a single innate motive, the tendency to actualize, maintain and enhance the self. Self-actualization is part of a broader actualization tendency covering all physiological and psychological needs.

Biologically, the tendency maintains the organism by meeting needs for food, water and safety. It begins in the womb, guiding the differentiation of organs and the development of physiological functions, and is responsible for maturation, the genetically determined development of the body from foetal growth to secondary sex characteristics at puberty. These changes are genetically programmed but brought to completion by the actualization tendency.

Psychologically, the same tendency pushes us to develop our abilities and potentials fully, with the goal of becoming a fully functioning person. It also broadens the infant's experiential world, eventually leading to the development of the self. Growth is not automatic or effortless: a child learning to walk falls and cries but keeps going, because the urge to actualize is stronger than the urge to regress. The organismic valuing process supports this by rating experiences that promote actualization as positive.

practice.q: What is the organismic valuing process?
practice.answer: The organismic valuing process is the process that governs behaviour throughout life, by which we judge experiences according to whether they foster or hinder actualization. Growth-promoting experiences get a positive value and are repeated; hindering ones get a negative value and are avoided, so it directly shapes behaviour.

practice.q: What is the experiential field? How does it change with age?
practice.answer:
The experiential field or world is the world of experience as each individual perceives it. Rogers treated it as a frame of reference that influences growth. We face countless stimuli, trivial and important, threatening and rewarding, and the reality of our environment depends on how we perceive it, which may not match objective reality. This is why personality can be understood only from the person's own viewpoint (a phenomenological approach).

The field differs between people: friends may react very differently to the same event, and a student may judge a roommate's behaviour differently from someone decades older. It also changes over time and circumstances; what a college student thinks is acceptable behaviour will probably change by the age of 70.

In infancy, as the actualization tendency drives growth, the experiential field broadens. Infants meet more sources of stimulation and respond to them as they subjectively perceive them, and experience becomes the basis for judgement and behaviour. Higher levels of development sharpen the field, and part of it eventually becomes differentiated as the self or self-concept.

practice.q: Explain Rogers's account of the development of the self in childhood, including positive regard, unconditional and conditional positive regard, positive self-regard, conditions of worth and incongruence. What parental behaviours affect the child's development?
practice.answer:
Introduction. For Rogers the self is the core of personality. His account of childhood explains how the self emerges from experience and how the reactions of others, especially the mother, determine whether the child grows toward full functioning or becomes incongruent and anxious.

Emergence of the self. As the infant's experiential field becomes more complex through widening social contact, one part becomes differentiated as 'I, me, myself': the self-concept. It separates what belongs to the self from external people, objects and events, and includes what we are, should be and would like to be. Ideally it is a consistent, organised whole, and behaviour that clashes with it is avoided.

Positive regard. As the self emerges, infants develop a need for positive regard: acceptance, love and approval from others, especially the mother. Rogers thought it probably learned but universal and persistent. Infants find it satisfying and its withdrawal frustrating. If the mother withholds it, actualization and self-development are hampered. Infants read disapproval of behaviour as disapproval of the self, and if this is frequent they stop striving for actualization and act instead to win approval, even against their self-concept. Positive regard is reciprocal: satisfying another person's need satisfies our own. Because it matters so much, we become sensitive to others' attitudes and internalise them in forming the self-concept.

Unconditional positive regard. When love persists despite undesirable behaviour, it is unconditional: given freely and fully, independent of what the child does. Rogers saw this as the ideal parental attitude.

Positive self-regard. In time positive regard comes from within; we learn to reward ourselves. A child loved for being happy will feel positive self-regard whenever behaving happily. Positive self-regard, contentment with oneself, is related to positive mental health (Leising and colleagues, 2013), and is also reciprocal, so those who have it may give positive regard to others.

Conditional positive regard and conditions of worth. Parents often withhold affection for behaviours that annoy, frighten or bore them. The infant learns that love has a price. If a parent is annoyed each time the infant drops things from the crib, the child learns to disapprove of himself for this; external standards become internal, the child punishes himself as the parent did, and the self-concept acts as a parental surrogate. The child develops conditions of worth: feeling worthy only when behaving in approved ways. Rogers compared this to Freud's superego. Such children no longer function freely; they evaluate and restrain themselves and so cannot fully actualize. Assor and Tai (2012) found that mothers' conditional regard for grades made adolescents' self-worth erratic.

Incongruence. Children may also deny or distort perceptions that conflict with these conditions. Experiences are now judged by whether they bring approval, not by whether they serve actualization. This creates incongruence between the self-concept and experience. Incongruent experiences are threatening and appear as anxiety: a person who sees herself as loving all humanity becomes anxious on feeling hatred, denies or distorts it, and part of her experiential field is closed off, making perceptions rigid.

Parental behaviours. Unconditional acceptance allows the child to avoid conditions of worth, remain congruent and open to experience, and move toward the good life. Research supports this: accepting, democratic, affectionate and rewarding parents have children with higher self-esteem, emotional security and creativity (Baldwin; Coopersmith; Harrington, Block, & Block), while conditional regard brings compliance but poor coping, unstable self-esteem and resentment (Assor, Roth, & Deci).

Conclusion. The development of the self thus hinges on the kind of regard a child receives. Unconditional positive regard leads to congruence and full functioning; conditional regard leads to conditions of worth, incongruence, anxiety and defensive distortion.

practice.q: Compare Rogers's concept of conditions of worth with Freud's concept of the superego.
practice.answer:
Rogers himself linked the two. He said positive self-regard, derived from conditional positive regard, is his version of the Freudian superego, and the textbook defines conditions of worth as similar to the superego.

Similarities. Both are internalised parental standards. In Rogers's account, when parents give affection only for certain behaviours, children absorb these standards; external judgement becomes internal, children punish themselves as parents did, and the self-concept functions as a parental surrogate. Like the superego, conditions of worth judge the self as good or bad, worthy or unworthy, in the parents' terms, and they restrain behaviour.

Differences. For Rogers the source is the experience of conditional love and approval, and the result is harmful: conditions of worth block actualization, produce incongruence and anxiety, and would not form at all under unconditional positive regard, which is the ideal. They are part of a conscious self-concept. The chapter's wider contrast also applies: Rogers saw people as conscious and rational, not ruled by unconscious forces or instincts, so his concept carries none of the instinctual conflict framework of Freud's theory.

practice.q: Describe Rogers's concept of incongruence. How is it related to anxiety?
practice.answer:
Incongruence is a discrepancy between a person's self-concept and aspects of his or her experience. It develops when children, living under conditions of worth, deny or distort unacceptable ways of perceiving their experiential world and start evaluating experiences by whether they win positive regard from others rather than by whether they serve the actualization tendency. Holding inaccurate perceptions, they risk becoming estranged from their true self.

Experiences that are incongruent with the self-concept are threatening and manifest as anxiety. Rogers's example: if my self-concept includes loving all humanity and I meet someone I hate, I become anxious, because hatred does not fit my image of myself as loving.

To maintain the self-concept I deny the hatred, defending against the anxiety by distorting the experience. This closes off part of my experiential field and makes some perceptions rigid. The opposite state, congruence, means seeing self and world as they are, being open to experience and emotionally healthy. Research confirms that large discrepancies between perceived and ideal self go with anxiety, insecurity, depression and low self-esteem.

practice.q: What are the characteristics of the fully functioning person? Describe the roles of the intellect, positive and negative feelings, and spontaneity. Can a fully functioning person be called self-actualized?
practice.answer:
Introduction. For Rogers the fully functioning person, his term for self-actualization or the development of all facets of the self, is the most desirable outcome of psychological development and social evolution. Such people received unconditional positive regard, have no conditions of worth, and are congruent, so nothing threatens their self-concept. Rogers described several characteristics, summarised in Table 10.1.

Awareness of all experience: the role of positive and negative feelings. Fully functioning persons deny or distort no experience; everything filters through to the self. With nothing to defend against, there is no defensiveness. They are open to positive feelings such as courage and tenderness and to negative ones such as fear and pain. They are more emotional in the sense of accepting a wider range of feelings and experiencing them more intensely. Negative feelings are not avoided but accepted as part of experience.

Living fully in every moment. Every experience is potentially fresh and new. Experiences are not predicted or anticipated but participated in fully rather than merely observed.

Trust in one's own organism: the role of the intellect. They trust their own reactions more than others' opinions, a social code or intellectual judgement; behaving in a way that feels right is a good guide to satisfying behaviour. Rogers did not mean they ignore their intellect or other people. All data, including intellectual reasoning and others' views, are accepted as congruent with the self-concept and weighed accurately. Decisions come from considering all experiential data, but because self and experience are congruent, the person is unaware of this weighing, so decisions appear more intuitive and emotional than intellectual. The intellect is thus integrated, not dominant.

Freedom of choice. They feel free to choose without constraints or inhibitions, which gives a sense of personal power: their future depends on their own actions, not circumstances, the past or other people, and they do not feel compelled to act in only one way.

Creativity and spontaneity. They live creatively, constructively and adaptively as conditions change. Spontaneity is allied with creativity: they are flexible, seek new experiences and challenges, and do not need predictability, security or freedom from tension.

Continual growth and a state of actualizing. Table 10.1 lists a continual need to grow and to maximise one's potential. Rogers deliberately described such people as actualizing, not actualized. 'Actualized' would imply a finished, static personality, whereas self-development is always in progress; being fully functioning is a direction, not a destination. If growth stops, the person loses spontaneity, flexibility and openness. The word 'becoming' in On Becoming a Person (1961) captures this.

Not always easy. Full functioning means constantly testing, growing and striving, a complex and challenging life. Rogers did not describe such people as happy or contented, though they may be at times; their lives are enriching, exciting and meaningful.

Can we call them self-actualized? Strictly, no. In Rogers's terms the fully functioning person is self-actualizing: always moving, never finished. To call someone self-actualized would contradict his emphasis on ongoing becoming.

Conclusion. The fully functioning person is open, present-focused, self-trusting, free, creative and forever growing. Feelings of all kinds are welcomed, the intellect is integrated into organismic trust, and spontaneity keeps growth alive.

practice.q: How does Rogers's image of human nature differ from Freud's? Would you call Rogers an optimist or a pessimist? What was his position on childhood versus adult experiences?
practice.answer:
Rogers favoured free will: fully functioning persons create their selves and nothing in personality is predetermined. On nature-nurture he stressed environment: the actualization tendency is innate, but actualizing is shaped more by social than biological forces. Childhood has some impact, but later experiences have greater influence, and present feelings matter more than childhood events. He saw some universality in the shared traits of fully functioning people, with room for uniqueness in expression, and the goal of life is to become fully functioning.

Freud, by contrast, stressed unconscious forces, biological instincts, inevitable conflict and the decisive role of the first five years. Rogers rejected all of these: we are not doomed to conflict with ourselves or society, not ruled by instincts, not controlled by early childhood. We are conscious, rational beings whose outlook is progressive rather than regressive.

Rogers was clearly an optimist. He believed people have a basically healthy nature and an innate tendency to grow, that emotional disturbances are uncommon, and that even destructive people have strongly positive directional tendencies. At 85 he said his work kept reinforcing his positive view. He also believed that as more people self-actualize, society improves.

practice.q: How does the clinical interview in Rogers's person-centred approach differ from the psychoanalytic clinical interview? What did Rogers call his approach and why?
practice.answer:
Rogers's approach was first called non-directive, then client-centred, and finally person-centred therapy. The name conveys that the ability to change and improve personality is centred in the person: the person, not the therapist, directs change, and the therapist only facilitates. He called those he helped clients, never patients.

In the person-centred interview the therapist explores the client's feelings and attitudes, listens without preconceptions and tries to see the client's experiential world as the client does. The only predetermined belief is the client's inherent worth. The therapist gives unconditional positive regard, makes no judgements and gives no advice; responsibility for change rests with the client. There is no predetermined theoretical structure into which problems must be fitted.

The psychoanalytic interview, by contrast, works within Freud's theory and uses free association, dream analysis and case histories. Rogers opposed these because they made clients dependent on the therapist as an authority, implied the therapist knew all about them, and removed personal responsibility. Rogers admitted his method learns only what clients consciously express and depends on their communication, but claimed it gives the clearest view of their experiential world.

practice.q: How does the Q-sort technique measure a person's self-image? What has Q-sort research shown about the self-concept before and after therapy, and what other research supports Rogers's theory?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Although Rogers said he learned nothing from research, he and his associates studied how the self-concept changes in therapy using qualitative and quantitative methods, including rating scales, content analysis of recorded sessions and, above all, the Q-sort technique. Later research has tested many of his other ideas.

The Q-sort technique. Developed by William Stephenson (1953), the Q-sort asks clients to sort a large number of self-descriptive statements, for example about enjoying being alone, feeling helpless or being emotionally mature, into categories from most to least descriptive. This empirically defines or quantifies the self-image. Clients can sort the same statements twice: once for the perceived self (how they see themselves) and once for the ideal self (who they would most like to be). Using correlation, Rogers measured how closely the two corresponded and how this changed from before to after therapy. A low correlation indicates incongruence; a higher one indicates greater congruence and emotional health.

Mrs. Oak. For this client the perceived-ideal correlation was +.36 before therapy and rose to +.79 a year after (Rogers, 1954). Before therapy she saw herself as dependent and passive and felt rejected, choosing statements about feeling driven, insecure, disorganised and needing excuses. Twelve months after therapy she felt closer to the self she wanted to be: secure, less fearful, emotionally mature, self-reliant, adequate and able to relate warmly to others. Rogers concluded her emotional health had improved.

Butler and Haigh (1954). In 25 clients the perceived-ideal discrepancy decreased during and after therapy; the average correlation rose from .01 to +.31.

Other research on therapy. Therapy works better when clients see their therapists as empathic, showing unconditional positive regard and congruent (Cain, 2013). The Experiencing Scale showed that clients who improved most gained most in self-trust (Klein and colleagues, 1969). A newer Sexual Satisfaction Q-Sort found four categories of sexual experience (McClelland, 2014).

Openness and adjustment. Chodorkoff (1954) compared students' self Q-sorts with clinicians' Q-sorts based on the TAT and Rorschach. Poorly adjusted students showed more perceptual defence against threatening words, and the closer the self and clinician descriptions, the better adjusted the student, supporting the idea that healthy people are open and see themselves accurately.

Acceptance of self and parental regard. Self-accepting mothers accepted their children more, and children's self-acceptance partly depended on mothers' (Medinnus & Curtis, 1963). Unconditionally accepting, democratic, affectionate parents had children with higher self-esteem, security and creativity (Baldwin; Coopersmith; Harrington, Block, & Block), while conditional regard brought compliance but poor coping, fluctuating self-esteem and resentment (Assor, Roth, & Deci, 2004) and made teens act against their true selves (Harter and colleagues, 1996).

Emotional adjustment. The greater the perceived-ideal discrepancy, the higher the anxiety, insecurity, depression and social incompetence, and the lower self-esteem and self-actualization; such people are seen as awkward and unfriendly. Ford (1991) found that a larger gap between childhood EAS temperament and adult self-perception predicted more maladjustment, supporting the idea that unrealised potential causes maladjustment. Some evidence supports the organismic valuing process, though positive self-regard may be less prevalent in collectivist cultures like Japan.

Conclusion. Q-sort research consistently shows perceived and ideal selves becoming more congruent after therapy, and wider research supports Rogers's views on congruence, openness, unconditional regard and adjustment.

practice.q: What do studies show about the results of parental use of conditional positive regard? How can parents' behaviour affect their children, according to Rogers?
practice.answer:
According to Rogers, parents who give unconditional positive regard let children develop without conditions of worth, so they remain congruent, open to experience and able to actualize. Parents who give conditional regard teach children that love has a price; children internalise conditions of worth, inhibit their behaviour, and may distort experience, leading to incongruence and anxiety.

Research on conditional regard: Assor, Roth, and Deci (2004) found it did produce the behaviours parents wanted, but children reported poor coping, fluctuating self-esteem, low self-worth, feelings of parental disapproval and resentment; children of parents who did not use it had none of these problems. Assor and Tai (2012) found mothers' conditional regard for grades made adolescents' self-worth erratic. Harter and colleagues (1996) found teens with conditional regard lacked confidence and hope and acted against their true selves to win approval.

Research on unconditional acceptance: accepting, democratic parents had children with higher self-esteem and security (Baldwin, 1949); affectionate, rewarding parents had high-self-esteem children (Coopersmith, 1967); unconditional regard with free expression fostered creativity (Harrington, Block, & Block, 1987); and self-accepting mothers accepted their children more (Medinnus & Curtis, 1963).

practice.q: What criticisms have been made of Rogers's theory, and why was person-centred therapy accepted so quickly?
practice.answer:
Criticisms. Rogers insisted personality could be explored only through person-centred therapy and clients' self-reports of subjective experience. Critics argue he therefore ignored factors outside conscious awareness that still influence behaviour. They also point out that self-reports can be distorted: people may repress some events and elaborate on or invent others to hide their true nature and present an idealised self-image.

Rapid acceptance. Social conditions after World War II in 1945 played a major role. Returning veterans needed help adjusting to civilian life, creating demand for psychologists and for a technique that could be learned and used quickly. Psychoanalysis required a medical degree and long training, whereas person-centred therapy was, as DeCarvalho put it, simple, informal, brief and needing little training. More than 400 college counselling centres based on Rogers's ideas were set up under the Veterans Administration, and hundreds more colleges opened their own. Rogers acknowledged that post-war stresses made him famous.

Despite the criticisms, the approach remains influential, used to train managers, psychologists, social workers and counsellors, with over 200 training centres and dozens of journals.

An encounter group is Rogers's group therapy technique in which 8 to 15 people, meeting 20 to 60 hours without a set agenda, learn about their feelings and how they relate to one another. A facilitator, not a leader, helps members gain self-insight and become more fully functioning.

practice.q: Distinguish between positive regard and positive self-regard.
practice.answer: Positive regard is acceptance, love and approval received from others, especially the mother in infancy. Positive self-regard develops later, when this approval comes from within: we grant ourselves acceptance and approval after internalising others' attitudes, in effect learning to reward ourselves.

practice.q: Why did Rogers describe the fully functioning person as 'actualizing' rather than 'actualized'?
practice.answer: 'Actualized' implies a finished, static personality, but for Rogers self-development is always in progress; full functioning is a direction, not a destination. If growth stops, spontaneity, flexibility and openness are lost, as the word 'becoming' in On Becoming a Person suggests.

The Q-sort, developed by William Stephenson, is a self-report technique in which a person sorts many self-descriptive statements into categories from most to least descriptive. Rogers used it to compare the perceived self with the ideal self and track how their correlation changed with therapy.

summary: Rogers developed person-centred therapy (earlier non-directive, then client-centred) from clinical experience, not laboratory research; the person, not the therapist, directs change.
People are conscious, rational beings; personality is understood phenomenologically, from the person's own subjective experience, and present feelings outweigh the past.
His lonely, strict religious childhood made him rely on his own experience; he linked his interest in therapy to that loneliness.
Kell's and McNeil's studies showed self-insight best predicted delinquent behaviour, making the self the core of his theory.
The single innate motive is the actualization tendency, which maintains the organism, drives maturation from the womb, and pushes psychological growth despite struggle.
The organismic valuing process rates experiences by whether they serve actualization; we seek positive ones and avoid negative ones.
Reality is the experiential world as perceived; it broadens in infancy and gives rise to the self-concept (what we are, should be and would like to be).
Infants need positive regard; unconditional positive regard is love regardless of behaviour, and positive self-regard is approval from within.
Conditional positive regard produces conditions of worth, similar to the superego, which inhibit free functioning and actualization.
Incongruence between self-concept and experience causes anxiety, defended against by denial and distortion; congruence means emotional health.
Fully functioning persons are open to all experience, live in the moment, trust their organism, feel free, are creative and spontaneous, and are always actualizing, not actualized.
Rogers's image of human nature is optimistic: free will, environment over heredity, present over past, some universality, growth over stagnation.
Assessment is through subjective experience in person-centred therapy with unconditional positive regard; Rogers rejected free association, dream analysis and case histories.
Encounter groups extended his approach to groups; others developed the Experience Inventory and Experiencing Scale.
Rogers pioneered recording therapy sessions; Q-sort research (Mrs. Oak, Butler & Haigh) showed perceived and ideal selves becoming more congruent after therapy.
Research supports links between unconditional regard and self-esteem, self-acceptance and acceptance of others, and between perceived-ideal discrepancy and maladjustment.
Criticisms: neglect of unconscious factors and reliance on distortable self-reports; post-WWII veterans' needs drove rapid acceptance, and the approach remains influential.
